transcript.content: Right, let's get into it. Thinking about where you actually spend time with your male friends — what's your favourite kind of place for that? Could be somewhere specific, could be a type of place. Why that one?

Yeah, I mean — for me it's a bit different, I suppose, because I work from home. I don't have that natural thing where you see blokes at work and you end up going for a drink after, or whatever. So it tends to be more planned, if that makes sense? I'll meet someone for a walk actually, quite often. There's some decent green spaces near us, local parks and that. It's... I dunno, it feels less forced than sitting in a pub, you know? You're doing something, you're talking while you're walking, and you can just chat without it being this big thing.

I think working from home changes it. You don't get that natural decompression time John was talking about — you sort of have to make it happen yourself. So meeting a mate for a walk is kind of two birds with one stone. You get out, you get your head cleared, and you've seen your mate. Pub's fine too, but there's something about just being outdoors that works better for me.

Yeah, that makes sense for you, Paul. But it's a bit different for me, to be honest. I'm already out all day driving between jobs, right? So by the time I've finished work, the last thing I fancy is going for a walk somewhere. I've been moving around since half six this morning — in the van, in and out of people's houses, carrying stuff. I'm not really needing to get out and decompress in that way.

For me it's actually the pub, if I'm seeing the lads. That's where I end up most of the time. It's the one place I'm actually sat down, not thinking about the next job or what I need to pick up from the van. Just... stationary, you know? With a pint, having a chat. That's decompression for me, because I've been on the move all day.

So I get what you're saying about needing that mental break — that's definitely real — but I reckon it depends what your day's already looked like. If you're home-based and you've been inside, a walk makes perfect sense. But if you've been driving round all day already, you just want to sit still somewhere.

No, that's a fair point, Nick. You're right — I hadn't thought of it that way. I mean, I'm sat at a desk most of the day, so yeah, moving around is what I need. But if you're already out and about all day like you are, then sitting down with a pint somewhere makes complete sense. That's the opposite of what I need, isn't it? You need to be stationary, I need to move. Fair enough.

Yeah, that's exactly it for me too, Nick. I'm in the van or driving between sites a fair bit with my role — not every day like you, but enough. And when I do get an evening where I can actually go out, the pub's where I'll head if I'm meeting someone. You've nailed it — you just want to sit still, haven't you? I'm not looking for another activity or to go for a walk or anything like that. I've been moving around, dealing with stuff at work, and by the time I get home and then head back out, I just want to be somewhere I can plant myself down.

The thing is, the pub's good because it doesn't demand anything of you either. You're not having to be actively doing something or heading somewhere. You're just... there. Having a pint, bit of a chat. No pressure. You can relax properly. That's different from what Paul's saying about the walk, but I reckon we're both after the same thing really — just decompressing after the day — we just need different things to get there.

Yeah, that's a good way of putting it — same destination, different routes. Right, let's move on and talk a bit more directly about food. I'm interested in how you all actually decide what to eat — day to day, week to week. How does that work for you?

Yeah, right — for me it's a bit mental if I'm honest. When you're out on site all day like I am, you haven't really got much choice a lot of the time. You're grabbing whatever's near the job — a sandwich from a van, a takeaway nearby, or you've made something at home in the morning and brought it with you. There's not a lot of planning goes into it.

Most days I'll just take a packed lunch — my wife sorts that out or I'll throw something together the night before. But if I'm working late or the job's running over, you end up just... stopping somewhere on the drive back, getting a burger or fish and chips or whatever's quickest. It's not ideal, but when you've been grafting since half six in the morning and you're tired, you're not thinking about balanced meals, are you? You just want something that fills you up quick.

Evenings are different — we'll have proper meals at home, but the daytime's just whatever works around the site. I think Nick probably gets that more than most of us here, being out in the van all day like you are. It's not like when you're in an office where you can plan ahead or go somewhere proper for lunch.

Yeah, exactly Daniel. It's the same story for me really. My wife usually does a packed lunch — sandwiches, bit of fruit, that sort of thing — and I'll take that with me. But honestly, half the time when I'm out on jobs, I don't even get to it properly. You're in someone's house doing an install, you can't exactly sit down for twenty minutes with a meal, can you? So you're just... grabbing something between jobs if you get a chance. Bit of a baguette from a shop, or if I've got time I'll stop at a cafe somewhere.

The problem is you never really know what your day's going to look like either. You think you've got time for a break and then a job runs over, or you're waiting for a part, or there's something that needs sorting on the previous job. By the time you've actually finished, you're starving and you just grab whatever's nearest — drive-thru, chippy, whatever.

It's not great, I know. The wife gives me a bit of stick about it sometimes. But when you're knackered and you've still got an hour's drive potentially to get back, you're not thinking about what's balanced or healthy. You just want something quick that'll keep you going til you get home for a proper meal. That's where the eating actually happens for us — evening time when we've all sat down together. The daytime stuff is just fuel, really.

Yeah, that's it exactly Nick. The wife does the same thing — makes sure I've got something with me, but she knows half the time it won't happen. She's given up lecturing me about it really, but you can tell she'd rather I wasn't grabbing a kebab on the way home.

The thing is, evenings are different though, aren't they? That's when you actually sit down and eat properly. Both of us make a point of that — we'll have a decent meal, it's not rushed. That's the one meal of the day that's actually... I dunno, intentional? You know what I mean? The midday stuff when you're on site is just keeping the engine running. But evening time, that's when it matters. We've got time, we're not going anywhere, you can actually taste what you're eating.

I reckon that's why the daytime stuff doesn't bother me as much as maybe it should. Because the real eating — the proper meals — that's still happening. It's just the bits in between that are a bit chaotic. Long as you're having a decent meal when you get home, you can get away with grabbing a sausage roll at lunchtime.

Yeah, I hear that. Though for me it's a bit more than just... you know, getting a decent meal in the evening. It's the time with my kid as well, to be honest. That's become the thing that matters, since we've had our little one.

I mean, I'm out all day like you Daniel, so I don't see much of them during the week. And by the time I get home, if I've stopped at a drive-thru or whatever, I've missed that window where they're actually awake and we can all sit down together. So now my wife and I are quite deliberate about it — we make sure there's a proper meal ready, we all eat together, even if it's just half an hour before bedtime routine kicks in. That's the bit of the day that actually feels... important, you know?

It changes how you think about the food thing. It's not just about whether you've had something to eat or not. It's about actually being present for that. So yeah, the midday stuff's still just whatever I can grab, but the evening meal — that's different. That's the one time in the day where we're all in one place and not rushing off somewhere else. That matters more now than it used to, if that makes sense.

Yeah, I get that Nick. That's fair enough. Though I'll be honest — we haven't got kids, so it's a bit different for us. The evening meal's still important, don't get me wrong, but it's not got that same... weight to it, if you know what I mean? It's nice to sit down together, my wife and I, but there's not that sense of it being the one time you actually see your kid during the day.

For us it's more just — you want a decent meal after work, you want to unwind a bit, and you're both there so you might as well do it properly rather than just eating in front of the telly. But it's not the same stakes as what you're talking about. You've got that whole thing of making sure you're present for your little one, and I can see why that would change how you think about the whole food situation. It makes sense.

That's an interesting distinction, Daniel — same habit, different reasons behind it. Okay, I want to shift gears slightly, because what you've all been describing touches on something I'd like to explore a bit more directly. Thinking about what you eat — not just when or where — do you reckon your gender plays any part in that? Does being a man shape what you eat, or how you think about food at all?

I don't know — I don't really think about it that way, to be honest. For me it's just practical, isn't it? You need to eat, you grab something that works with what you're doing that day. But now you mention it... I suppose there's maybe something there in what Daniel and Nick were saying. They both sounded like they were almost apologizing for not planning it properly, or for just grabbing whatever's quickest. And I recognise that — that thing of not wanting to fuss about it too much.

I mean, I live on my own, so it's a bit different — I'm not answering to anyone about what I'm eating like Daniel's wife might have thoughts about the kebab, or Nick's trying to be home for the family meal. But even so, I don't sit around thinking about menus or nutrition or any of that. I'll make something straightforward in the evening, take something with me during the week, and that's... that's fine, isn't it? It gets done.

I reckon maybe there is something gender-shaped in not wanting to deliberate over it too much, or treating it as just fuel rather than something to think deeply about. But that's not really how I'd frame it — it's more just how you are when you're working long hours and you're tired. You want it simple and quick. Whether that's a bloke thing or just a tired person thing, I'm not sure.

I think there's something in what you're saying, Andrew, but I'd push back a bit on the "just tired" thing. Because I've noticed — looking back at my own life anyway — that when you get into that habit of just treating it as fuel, you kind of... stop noticing what that costs you, don't you?

I mean, I did exactly what you lot are describing for years. Out early, grab whatever, home late, eaten something or not. And you tell yourself it's fine, it's just fuel, it's practical. But then at some point I started actually sitting down with a meal — not even anything fancy, just actually sitting and eating it rather than wolfing it down in the van or at the desk. And I realised I'd been... I don't know, half-starving myself without really clocking it. Not in a dramatic way, just sort of missing something.

And yeah, I reckon there's a bloke thing in it. There's that bit where you don't want to think too hard about what you're eating, like it's a bit soft or something. You just want it to be fuel, practical, done. But I think we've normalized that so much that we don't actually realize we've opted out of something. Like — Nick's got his family meal in the evening, and that's when it becomes something, doesn't it? It becomes time together rather than just eating. But for a lot of us, it's just... never that. It's just functional.

I've found lately that actually taking time to eat, even just on my own, it's become one of the few bits where you can actually slow down. That decompression thing we were talking about earlier — for me it's often actually been sitting down with a proper meal. But I'm not sure I'd have noticed that if I hadn't stopped and thought about it.

Yeah, that's... fair point actually, John. I hear what you're saying. I hadn't really thought about it like that — the bit about not noticing what you're missing. I mean, you're right, I do just treat it as fuel most of the time. Get something in, move on. And I suppose I've never really stopped to ask myself whether that's actually... okay, or if there's something in it I'm just not clocking.

The thing is, living on my own, I could sit down and have a proper meal if I wanted to. There's nothing stopping me. But most evenings I'm just... I don't know, a bit flat when I get back. Telly on, something quick, and that's it. I've never really thought of it as missing something though. It's more just — that's how it works when you're knackered.

But you're saying that when you actually did stop and sit with it, it became different? Like actually noticing what you're eating rather than just... doing it? I suppose I can see that. And maybe there's a bit of — I don't know, stubbornness in it? Where you don't want to make a fuss about food because that feels like something else, something less practical. But if what you're saying is you actually felt better when you stopped rushing it...

I'm not sure I'd describe it like you are, but I think I get what you mean. It's not about the food itself, it's about actually stopping.

Yeah, that's it exactly. It's not about becoming someone who cares about food or anything like that. It's just — you're actually there, aren't you? You're not halfway through something else, not thinking about the next thing.

I mean, I still do the quick stuff most days. I'm not suddenly cooking fancy meals or anything daft like that. But on an evening when I've actually sat down — even if it's just toast and beans or whatever — I notice I'm... calmer, I suppose? Less wound up. Your head stops spinning for a minute.

And look, I'm not saying it changed my life or anything. I'm still working long hours, still tired. But that flat feeling you're describing, Andrew — I had that too. Just coming home and everything's a bit grey, you know? And I think part of that was just never actually stopping, never actually being present in your own evening. You're eating but you're not eating. You're there but you're not really there.

So yeah, when you do actually sit with it, you notice. You taste it, you're not rushing off somewhere in your head. It's a small thing, but it does something. Nothing dramatic. Just — you're properly in your evening instead of just getting through it.

John, Andrew — that thing you're both describing, the 'not wanting to fuss about food' instinct, the stubbornness in it, the 'soft' word John used — I'm curious what Daniel, Nick, Paul make of that. Does that land for any of you? And specifically — does it feel like a bloke thing to you, or something else?

I think... yeah, there's something in it for me too, actually. Not the same way as what you lot are describing though, because my situation's different — I'm at home, so I've got time theoretically. But I've noticed the same thing that Andrew was saying, that flatness. You're sat at your desk working, you just grab something between calls, eat it without really noticing, and then you're back to work. And the day's kind of... grey, you know?

I hadn't connected it to the gender thing particularly until John said it, but yeah — I reckon there is something there. This idea that it's a bit fussy or self-indulgent to actually think about food, to sit down properly with it. Like that's not what you do, that's not practical. You just fuel up and get on.

But working from home, I've noticed it more because the days are quite flat anyway when you're not going anywhere. And if you're not actually stopping to eat — like, actually stopping, not just eating at your desk while you're answering emails — then your whole day just kind of blurs together. There's no rhythm to it.

I've started doing it differently in the last year or so. Just stepping away from the desk, having my lunch properly rather than eating while I'm working. And it does make a difference. Not a big thing, but you do feel a bit more... I dunno, anchored? Like you've actually had a break rather than just kept going.

So I think John's onto something. I don't think it's that we've got anything against food or we're being deliberately stubborn. It's more just — you don't want to make a fuss, you want to be efficient, get through the day. But then you end up not really noticing you're living it.

Paul, that's useful — the WFH angle on it is different but you're landing in the same place. So there's something in common there: this idea that making a fuss about food feels like it's not what you do. I want to push on that a bit with all of you — because I'm thinking about specific foods now, not just the act of eating. Like, if one of your mates said they were going vegetarian or vegan — does that carry any of that same 'soft' or 'fussy' charge? Or is it something else entirely? Daniel, Nick — you've been quiet on this one, curious what you make of it.

Hold on — I think we need to separate those out, because they're not the same thing at all, are they?

What we've been talking about — sitting down and actually eating, noticing your food instead of just wolfing it down — that's not the same as someone saying they're vegetarian or vegan. That's a completely different conversation.

I mean, yeah, there's probably a bloke thing where if someone said they weren't eating meat, there'd be some... I don't know, eyebrow-raising maybe. That joke about it being a bit precious or whatever. But that's about the dietary choice itself, not about taking time to eat properly. Those are two separate things and I don't think we should muddy them together.

What I'm talking about — what Paul's talking about — that's just slowing down enough to actually be there when you're eating. You can do that with a steak sandwich or beans on toast or a salad or whatever. That's not fussy, that's just... noticing. It's practical in its own way.

But if someone's chosen not to eat meat, that's a whole other thing. That's them making a decision about what goes on their plate. And yeah, there might be some resistance to that in bloke culture or whatever you want to call it. But don't mix it up with what we were saying. One's about the pace and the mindfulness of eating. The other's about what you're actually eating.

Fair point, John — those are two different things and I shouldn't have run them together. So let's stay on the one you just flagged: that eyebrow-raising, 'a bit precious' reaction when someone says they're not eating meat. You named it and then moved on from it — but that's actually the bit I want to pull at. Daniel, Nick — what do you make of that? Does that reaction ring true to you, and if so, what's actually behind it?

Yeah, look — it does ring true, to be honest. And I think John's right that it's different from what we were saying about just sitting down and eating properly. But the eyebrow-raising thing, that's real.

I mean, I work in people's homes all day, right? You get talking to customers while you're doing jobs, and you do hear it — someone mentioning their son or daughter's gone vegetarian, and there's that bit of... I dunno, a slight thing, isn't there? Not aggressive or anything, but that undertone of it being a choice, a statement almost. Like you're opting out of what normal people do.

And I reckon some of that does come from this idea of not making a fuss, not being different just for the sake of it. Because in the trades, you don't want to be the bloke who's difficult about stuff. You want to fit in, be straightforward, not cause bother. So if someone's saying they can't eat certain things or they've chosen not to, there's maybe a bit of — I dunno — wariness? Like, are they going to be difficult on a job site, are they going to need special meals, is this going to be a thing?

But saying that out loud, I'm not sure that's fair, is it? It's just a choice someone's made. My wife's been cutting back on meat actually, and I don't give her stick about it. It just is what it is. But yeah, that initial reaction — that slight eyebrow thing — I recognize it. And I think it probably does come from this not-wanting-to-make-a-fuss culture that we were talking about. Because if you're the bloke who doesn't fuss about food, then someone who does fuss — who's deliberate about it — that maybe feels a bit... alien? Different?
Nick, that thing you said about the trades — not wanting to be the bloke who's difficult — that's a specific way of putting it. Daniel, you're in construction. Does that land with you?

Yeah, it does actually. You don't want to be the one who's causing complications on a job, that's just how it is. You're working with the same crew sometimes, or moving between sites, and everyone's trying to get the work done. You don't want to be marked as the awkward one.

But I'd say it's less about the vegetarian thing specifically and more just — you want to pull your weight, not stand out in a way that makes things slower or harder. If someone on site said they didn't eat meat, I don't think anyone would give them a hard time about it exactly. But there'd be that bit of... I suppose it's the practicality thing we were talking about, isn't it? Like, why would you make things more complicated for yourself? Just eat what's there.

I don't think it's malicious or anything. It's more just — you're used to a certain way of doing things. Straightforward, efficient. So when someone does something differently, there's maybe a moment of not quite getting it. But that's different from actually thinking they're soft or whatever.

Though I'll be honest — I can't think of anyone on the sites I work on who's vegetarian. It's not really a thing in construction, not in my experience anyway. So I'm not sure if that's because people who work in the trades just don't tend to be, or whether someone who was wouldn't really advertise it. Hard to say.
That last bit you said, Daniel — 'wouldn't really advertise it.' Do you think it's that there genuinely aren't vegetarians in construction, or that if there were, they'd keep it quiet?

I reckon it's probably a bit of both, isn't it? I mean, the work itself attracts a certain type of person — people who are practical, want to get things done, not overthinking stuff. So maybe that filters naturally towards people who aren't going to be bothered about what they eat. But also... yeah, if someone did feel that way, they probably wouldn't make a big deal about it on site. You'd just bring your own lunch or whatever, not announce it.

It's not like anyone would turn on them or anything. But there's that thing of not standing out, not being the one who needs special treatment or has different requirements. You just get on with it quietly if you need to. So whether there actually aren't many vegetarians in construction or whether they just keep their heads down — I couldn't tell you which it is really.

Daniel, that 'keep your head down' framing is a useful place to land — it's not about being attacked, it's just about not making yourself conspicuous. Right, we've covered a lot of ground on how gender shapes the way men relate to food and what gets flagged as different or fussy. I want to move us on, because there's something I'd like to actually put to all of you directly. Imagine you decided to go plant-based — just for the sake of the conversation, whether or not it's something you'd actually do. What would need to change in your life for that to be a realistic thing?

Right, yeah — that's different from just talking about it, isn't it? Because it's not really about the cultural thing at that point, it's about what actually has to shift practically.

For me, I think the first thing would be — I'd need time to plan it. Because right now, the way I work, I'm grabbing whatever's near a job or I've got something my mate threw together the night before. If I went plant-based, that doesn't work anymore. I'd have to actually think about what I'm taking with me, make sure there's something decent to eat. Can't just stop at a garage and grab a sausage roll.

So it'd mean — more planning in the morning, probably. Which sounds simple, but when you're up at four in the morning anyway and you're knackered, that's an actual barrier, isn't it? It's not just the choice itself, it's all the infrastructure around it that would have to change.

And then there's the evening meals. At the moment, I don't really cook — my housemate and I, we just sort of... manage. But if I was plant-based, I'd probably need to actually learn what I'm doing in the kitchen, or at least know enough to put together meals that aren't just beans on toast every night. That takes time and attention that I'm not currently giving to food.

So yeah — it's not the eyebrow-raising thing that would stop me. It's just the actual logistics of it. You'd need to shift from treating food as something that happens to you, to something you actually have to manage. And when you're already working fifty-hour weeks, that's... it's a real thing, not just a stubbornness thing.

Yeah, but I think — I mean, John's right about the practical side of it, all that planning and learning to cook properly. That's real. But I'd push back a bit on what he's saying about it being just logistics, because I don't think it's that simple, is it?

Like, I live on my own. I've got spare rooms, I've got time in the evenings if I wanted to use it. There's nothing actually stopping me from sitting down and planning meals or learning to cook something decent. And honestly, if I decided tomorrow I was going plant-based, the practical side — the planning, the cooking — that wouldn't be as much of a barrier for me as it might be for John with his early starts and all that.

But I still wouldn't do it. And when I think about why... it's not just tiredness, is it? It's more that I don't really want to think about food that hard. And I think — and this is what's been sitting with me from what you were saying earlier, John — I'm using the practicality thing as a cover for not wanting to engage with it at all.

Because you're right. There's something in the culture where you don't fuss about what you eat, and I've bought into that. And part of me not wanting to do it isn't because I can't, it's because it feels like — I dunno, it feels like something I shouldn't be bothered with. Like that's not what I do. So I just... don't. And then I tell myself it's because I'm too tired or it's not practical, when actually I haven't really tried.

Yeah, but Andrew — I think you're conflating two different things there, and I'm not sure that's fair on either of us, to be honest.

You're right that you've got the time and the space to learn to cook, to plan it out. You could do that. But what I'm talking about — the practicality thing for me — that's not an excuse. That's an actual constraint. I'm up at four, I'm working fifty-hour weeks, I'm grabbing meals in between jobs. I don't have the space to mess about experimenting with food right now, whether I wanted to or not.

But that's different from what you're describing. You're saying you don't want to think about food that hard, and you're using tiredness or practicality as the reason. That's... yeah, that might be a bit of avoidance on your part. But me saying I haven't got time to completely change how I eat and plan my weeks — that's not the same thing. That's just my actual life right now.

I'm not saying the cultural thing isn't there. It is. I get not wanting to fuss about it. But I think there's a difference between "I could do this if I really wanted to but I don't want to think about it" and "I literally don't have the bandwidth to restructure my working day around meal planning." Those aren't the same barrier, and I don't think we should pretend they are.

So there's a real distinction on the table there — John's describing something structural, baked into how his day works, and Andrew's describing something more like a choice not to engage. What do the rest of you make of that split? When you think about what would actually need to change for you to go plant-based — does it land closer to John's side of that, or Andrew's, or somewhere else entirely?

I think — for me it's actually a bit different from both of you, and I've been sitting with that while you've been talking.

Because I've got what looks like Andrew's situation, right? I'm at home, I've got the time, there's nothing practically stopping me. But the thing I've realized is that working from home has actually created its own kind of... structural thing, I suppose.

Like, when you go to an office or you're on a site, there's a moment where you have to stop. You break for lunch, there's a rhythm to the day that forces you to think about food. But when you're at home, especially when you're working, that just... doesn't happen. There's no trigger point. You're at your desk, you grab something between emails, you don't even register doing it. And because there's no natural break built in, it becomes invisible, doesn't it?

So yeah, I could theoretically plan meals and learn to cook properly like Andrew's saying. But the reason I haven't is partly what he's describing — not wanting to think about it too much — but it's also that the structure of my day doesn't even ask the question in the first place. There's no moment where I have to decide what to eat because I'm just... never really stopping.

So if I went plant-based, what would actually need to change isn't just the planning. It's me having to deliberately create those stopping points, those trigger points that other people get naturally from how their work is structured. And that's harder than it sounds, because you're building something that doesn't exist yet, rather than just working around something that's already there.

Does that make sense? It's structural, but in a different way.

Yeah, that does make sense, Paul. And I think you're onto something there that's actually harder than what I was describing, if I'm honest.

Because what you're saying — you'd have to actively choose to stop, to create those moments. And that's... that takes a different kind of effort, doesn't it? I mean, my day's structured for me by the work itself. I've got to be at a job at a certain time, I've got to finish it, move to the next one. The stopping points are there whether I like it or not. I'm not choosing to break — I'm forced to.

But you're saying you'd have to decide to do that. You'd have to say, "Right, I'm stopping now, I'm having lunch now," when there's nothing actually making you. And then you'd have to do that consistently, every day, even when you're tired or you're in the middle of something. That's... yeah, that's potentially harder than just working around the structure you've already got.

I hadn't really thought about it that way. I've been thinking about my constraints as the thing that makes it difficult.
